original_question: Characterize the Krylov intersection and Krylov reducibility for Friedrichs operators. In the bounded setting, the Krylov intersection is I(A, g) = K(A, g) ∩ A(K(A, g)^⊥); in the unbounded setting, when the Krylov subspace is defined, the corresponding expression is I(A, g) = K(A, g) ∩ A(K(A, g)^⊥ ∩ dom A). Krylov reducibility asks whether K(A, g)^⊥ is also invariant under A, equivalently whether A K(A, g)^⊥ ⊂ K(A, g)^⊥. The problem is to determine these structures both for abstract Friedrichs operators on Hilbert space and, concretely, for the classical Friedrichs differential operator.
target_in_paper: Section 4, Question 5: "To characterise the Krylov intersection relative to an abstract Friedrichs operator acting in a Hilbert space and a vector (see (2.8) and (2.9) above), as well as the Krylov reducibility of A (as in the spirit of Proposition 2.1). Or, at the concrete level, to characterise the Krylov intersection and the Krylov reducibility of the classical Friedrichs operator (3.1)."
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies Question 5 as being about the Krylov intersection and Krylov reducibility, it gives the bounded and unbounded formulas corresponding to (2.8) and (2.9), it correctly interprets reducibility through invariance of K(A,g)^perp, and it matches the paper's two levels of interest: abstract Friedrichs operators on Hilbert space and the classical Friedrichs differential operator.
missing_details: The paper's official formulation is an open problem labeled Question 5 in Section 4, and it is explicitly presented as a structural question rather than as a general classification program.
The ambient space is a complex Hilbert space H.

The paper's abstract Friedrichs setting is not an arbitrary operator class: it comes from a joint pair of closed densely defined operators satisfying the Friedrichs conditions (3.3), namely the Hilbert-space Friedrichs framework reviewed in Section 3.
To make the unbounded case stand-alone, one must state the domain hypothesis needed for the Krylov subspace to exist: g must belong to dom(A^n) for every n >= 0.
The Krylov subspace itself should be stated explicitly as K(A,g) = span{A^n g : n in N_0}.

For the concrete side, the classical Friedrichs operator must be identified more explicitly: on a bounded Lipschitz domain Omega subset R^d, with matrix-valued coefficients A_1,...,A_d and C satisfying the standard Friedrichs symmetry/coercivity assumptions of (3.1)-(3.2).

The nearby context says the main structural aim is especially to understand when the Krylov intersection is trivial, because Proposition 2.4 makes triviality of the intersection a sufficient criterion for Krylov solvability under suitable hypotheses.

The paper frames the expectation narrowly: the special Friedrichs constraints, abstractly (3.3) or concretely (3.1)-(3.2), should force special behavior of Krylov reducibility and/or of the triviality of the Krylov intersection.

Your draft slightly over-formalizes reducibility in a way that is fully standard in the bounded setting; the paper itself phrases Question 5 more cautiously as characterizing reducibility "in the spirit of Proposition 2.1," while explicitly referencing both (2.8) and (2.9).
refined_question: Let H be a complex Hilbert space, let A be an abstract Friedrichs operator in the sense of Section 3, i.e. a closed realization arising from a joint pair of closed densely defined operators satisfying the Friedrichs conditions (3.3), and let g in H; in the unbounded case assume g belongs to dom(A^n) for every n >= 0, so that the Krylov subspace K(A,g) := span{A^n g : n in N_0} is well defined. Characterize, under these Friedrichs constraints, the Krylov intersection I(A,g) := K(A,g) ∩ A(K(A,g)^perp) in the bounded case and I(A,g) := K(A,g) ∩ A(K(A,g)^perp ∩ dom A) in the unbounded case, and characterize the Krylov reducibility of A relative to g; in particular, determine when I(A,g) = {0}, since the paper singles out triviality of the Krylov intersection as the relevant structural condition for Krylov solvability. Carry out the analogous characterization for the classical Friedrichs operator of (3.1), namely the first-order differential operator T u = sum_{k=1}^d partial_k(A_k u) + C u on L^2(Omega; C^r), where Omega is a bounded Lipschitz domain and the matrix coefficients satisfy the Friedrichs symmetry/coercivity condition (3.2).
justification: The draft is targeting Question 5 exactly, not a neighboring problem. Question 5 verbatim asks for the characterization of the Krylov intersection and Krylov reducibility for abstract Friedrichs operators and, concretely, for the classical Friedrichs operator. Sections 2.2 and 2.3 provide the precise bounded and unbounded definitions of the Krylov intersection that your draft already reproduces, Section 3 supplies the abstract and classical Friedrichs frameworks, and the two sentences immediately following Question 5 explain that the intended emphasis is structural, especially the triviality of the Krylov intersection as a route to Krylov solvability. There is no numbered Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3 in this paper, so Question 5 is the nearest official formulation.
